name: Dogri

ancestors.notes: Descent from Old Indo-Aryan (Sanskrit) via Apabhraṃśa; Northwestern (Punjabic) Indo-Aryan zone.
Close contact/typological affinity with Punjabi, including the shared trait of lexical tone arising from lost breathy-voiced (murmured) obstruents.
Devanagari letter-to-sound conventions follow the Standard Hindi reading (schwa inherent vowel).

notes: Dogri, spoken mainly in Jammu (Jammu & Kashmir) and Himachal Pradesh, India. Northwestern Indo-Aryan (Punjabic group), officially written in Devanagari since standardisation (also historically in Takri/Dogra Akkhar script). Unusually for an Indo-Aryan language, Dogri is tonal: Bahri (2001) and Ghai (1991) describe a high-falling tone on word-initial historically-breathy-voiced consonants (घ झ ढ ध भ ढ़) and a low-rising tone on the preceding vowel when the breathy consonant is medial/final -- the same diachronic source (loss of murmured/breathy voicing, redistributed as pitch) documented for Punjabi. This tonogenesis is not encoded as separate grapheme keys here: the Devanagari letters that trigger it are exactly the aspirated/breathy-voiced series already mapped (identical to Hindi's), so the tone is a rule-layer fact about those letters' position, not a distinct spelling; representing it correctly needs a tone/pitch rule keyed to obstruent-breathiness plus syllable position, which is a candidate for allophone_rules once a citable rule-by-rule tonal grammar is available. Left as basic tier pending that.
